chapters.title: Cell Division

content.overview:
Cell division produces new cells for growth, repair and reproduction. Mitosis usually produces two genetically similar
 daughter cells, whereas meiosis reduces chromosome number and produces genetically varied cells for sexual
 reproduction.
key_terms: Interphase includes G1, S and G2; DNA is replicated during S phase.
Mitosis proceeds through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.
Meiosis consists of two divisions after one DNA replication; homologous chromosomes pair in prophase I.
Crossing over and independent assortment contribute to genetic variation.
study_notes: Interphase includes G1, S and G2; DNA is replicated during S phase.
Mitosis proceeds through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.
Meiosis consists of two divisions after one DNA replication; homologous chromosomes pair in prophase I.
Crossing over and independent assortment contribute to genetic variation.
Uncontrolled cell-cycle regulation can contribute to tumour formation.
content.short_questions:
What is mitosis?

    Answer: Mitosis is nuclear division that normally produces two daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as
    the parent nucleus.

 What is crossing over?

    Answer: Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of
    homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
content.long_questions:
Differentiate between mitosis and meiosis.

    Answer: Mitosis involves one nuclear division and normally produces two genetically similar cells with the same
    chromosome number as the parent. It supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis involves two
    successive divisions after one DNA replication and normally produces four haploid cells. Homologous pairing, crossing
    over and independent assortment occur in meiosis, creating variation and reducing chromosome number for sexual
    reproduction.

DNA replication occurs mainly during which part of the cell cycle? A. G1 phase B. S phase C. G2 phase D. M phase Answer: B

 and nucleic acids support cell structure, energy transfer, catalysis and inheritance.
key_terms: Carbohydrates provide energy and structural materials; monosaccharides are their simplest units.
Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds and perform structural, transport and catalytic roles.
Lipids include fats, oils, phospholipids and steroids; many are hydrophobic.

content.short_questions:
What is an enzyme?

    Answer: An enzyme is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up a chemical reaction without being
    consumed.

 What is a peptide bond?

    Answer: A peptide bond is the covalent bond that links the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of

content.long_questions:

    Answer: Enzyme activity depends on temperature, pH, substrate concentration and enzyme concentration. Activity
    generally rises with temperature to an optimum, after which denaturation reduces activity. Each enzyme has an
    optimum pH. Increasing substrate concentration raises the rate until active sites become saturated. Inhibitors may
    reduce activity by binding to the active site or another site.

chapters.title: Microorganisms

content.overview:
Microorganisms include viruses, bacteria, protozoa and microscopic fungi. They influence health, ecosystems, food
 production and industry. Some cause disease, while others recycle nutrients or are useful in biotechnology.
key_terms: Viruses are acellular and replicate only inside suitable host cells.
Bacteria are prokaryotes; their DNA is not enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus.
Bacteria may reproduce by binary fission and exchange genes through mechanisms such as conjugation.
Protozoa are eukaryotic; Plasmodium causes malaria and is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
study_notes: Viruses are acellular and replicate only inside suitable host cells.
Bacteria are prokaryotes; their DNA is not enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus.
Bacteria may reproduce by binary fission and exchange genes through mechanisms such as conjugation.
Protozoa are eukaryotic; Plasmodium causes malaria and is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
Microorganisms are used in fermentation, medicine, agriculture and waste treatment.
content.short_questions:
Why are viruses called obligate intracellular parasites?

    Answer: They can reproduce only inside living host cells because they depend on host-cell machinery.

 What causes malaria?

    Answer: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species, which are transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected
    female Anopheles mosquito.
content.long_questions:
Describe the main differences between bacteria and viruses.

    Answer: Bacteria are living prokaryotic cells with cellular organisation, cytoplasm, ribosomes and genetic material;
    many reproduce independently by binary fission. Viruses are acellular particles containing DNA or RNA within a protein
    coat, sometimes with an envelope. They lack their own metabolism and ribosomes and replicate only inside host cells.
    Antibiotics may act against susceptible bacteria but do not treat viral infections.

chapters.title: Algae and Fungi

content.overview:
Algae are mostly photosynthetic organisms, while fungi are heterotrophs that absorb nutrients. Both groups include
 organisms important in aquatic ecosystems, decomposition, food chains and human use.

key_terms: Algae may be unicellular, colonial or multicellular and contain photosynthetic pigments.
Fungal cell walls commonly contain chitin; their bodies are often made of hyphae forming a mycelium.
Fungi obtain nutrients by absorption and commonly reproduce by spores.
Lichens are associations between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner such as an alga or cyanobacterium.
study_notes: Algae may be unicellular, colonial or multicellular and contain photosynthetic pigments.

What is mycelium?

    Answer: Mycelium is the network or mass of thread-like fungal hyphae that forms the vegetative body of many fungi.

 What is a lichen?

    Answer: A lichen is a close association between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually an alga or
    cyanobacterium.
content.long_questions:
Explain the ecological importance of algae and fungi.

    Answer: Algae are primary producers in aquatic ecosystems, releasing oxygen and forming the base of many food
    webs. Some are used as food, fertilisers and industrial raw materials. Fungi decompose dead organic matter, recycle
    nutrients, form beneficial associations such as mycorrhizae, and are used in food production and medicine. Some
    algae and fungi can also cause harmful blooms, spoilage or disease.

chapters.title: Bryophyta and Pteridophyta

content.overview:
Bryophytes are small non-vascular plants that usually require water for fertilisation. Pteridophytes are vascular plants that
 reproduce by spores and possess true roots, stems and leaves.
key_terms: Bangladesh HSC Biology | First & Second Paper                                                                                       Page 8
Bryophytes lack true vascular tissues and have a dominant gametophyte generation.
The bryophyte sporophyte remains attached to and nutritionally dependent on the gametophyte.
Pteridophytes possess xylem and phloem and have a dominant sporophyte generation.
Both groups reproduce by spores rather than seeds.
study_notes: Bryophytes lack true vascular tissues and have a dominant gametophyte generation.
The bryophyte sporophyte remains attached to and nutritionally dependent on the gametophyte.
Pteridophytes possess xylem and phloem and have a dominant sporophyte generation.
Both groups reproduce by spores rather than seeds.
Water is generally required for motile male gametes to reach the egg.
content.short_questions:
Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom?

    Answer: They live mainly on land but require water for fertilisation because their motile male gametes must reach the
    egg.

 What is a sorus?

    Answer: A sorus is a cluster of sporangia, commonly found on the underside of fern leaves.
content.long_questions:
Compare bryophytes and pteridophytes.

    Answer: Bryophytes are non-vascular and lack true roots, stems and leaves; their gametophyte is the dominant
    generation and the sporophyte depends on it. Pteridophytes have vascular tissues and true organs; the sporophyte is
    dominant and independent. Both reproduce by spores and generally require water for fertilisation.

chapters.title: Gymnosperms and Angiosperms

content.overview:
Seed plants reproduce through pollen and ovules. Gymnosperms bear naked seeds, usually on cones, while
 angiosperms produce flowers and seeds enclosed within fruits.
key_terms: Gymnosperms do not form true fruits; their ovules are not enclosed in an ovary.
Angiosperms produce flowers; after fertilisation the ovary commonly develops into a fruit.
Bangladesh HSC Biology | First & Second Paper                                                                                       Page 9
In angiosperms, double fertilisation produces a zygote and endosperm.
Monocots typically have one cotyledon and parallel leaf venation; eudicots typically have two cotyledons and net venation.

content.short_questions:
What is double fertilisation?

    Answer: In angiosperms, one male gamete fuses with the egg to form a zygote, while the other fuses with the polar
    nuclei to form endosperm.

 What is a gymnosperm?

    Answer: A gymnosperm is a seed-producing plant whose seeds are not enclosed within a fruit.
content.long_questions:
Distinguish between gymnosperms and angiosperms.

    Answer: Gymnosperms bear exposed or naked ovules and seeds, commonly on cone scales, and do not produce true
    flowers or fruits. Angiosperms produce flowers; ovules are enclosed in an ovary and seeds are enclosed in fruits after
    development. Double fertilisation and endosperm formation are characteristic of angiosperms.

content.overview:

chapters.title: Human Physiology: Respiration and Breathing

content.overview:
Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs, while cellular respiration releases energy from nutrients. Gas exchange
 occurs across thin respiratory surfaces and is supported by ventilation and circulation.
key_terms: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens; thoracic volume increases.
Gas exchange in alveoli occurs by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients.
Oxygen is transported mainly bound to haemoglobin.
Carbon dioxide is transported mainly as bicarbonate ions in blood.
study_notes: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens; thoracic volume increases.
Gas exchange in alveoli occurs by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients.

content.short_questions:
Distinguish breathing and cellular respiration.

    Answer: Breathing is the physical movement of air into and out of the lungs; cellular respiration is the series of
    chemical reactions that release energy from organic molecules in cells.

 Why are alveoli efficient for gas exchange?

    Answer: Alveoli provide a large surface area, thin moist walls, a rich capillary supply and ventilation that maintains
    diffusion gradients.

chapters.title: Human Physiology: Waste and Excretion

content.overview:
Excretion removes metabolic wastes and helps regulate water, salts and pH. In humans, kidneys filter blood and form
 urine through filtration, reabsorption and secretion.
key_terms: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
Ultrafiltration occurs at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.
Selective reabsorption returns useful substances and much water to blood.
Tubular secretion transfers selected substances from blood into the nephron.
study_notes: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
Ultrafiltration occurs at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.

content.short_questions:
What is a nephron?

    Answer: A nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney, consisting of a renal corpuscle and renal tubule.

 What is ultrafiltration?

    Answer: Ultrafiltration is pressure-driven filtration of water and small solutes from glomerular blood into Bowman's
    capsule.
content.long_questions:
Describe the main steps of urine formation.

    Answer: Blood is filtered under pressure in the glomerulus, forming filtrate in Bowman's capsule. Along the renal
    tubule, useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, ions and much water are selectively reabsorbed. Additional
    ions and wastes may be secreted into the tubule. The collecting ducts adjust water reabsorption, and the final urine
    passes to the renal pelvis, ureter and bladder.

chapters.title: Human Physiology: Locomotion and Movement

content.overview:
Movement depends on the coordinated action of bones, joints, skeletal muscles and the nervous system. The skeleton
 supports and protects the body, while muscles generate force by contracting.
key_terms: The axial skeleton includes the skull, vertebral column and thoracic cage; the appendicular skeleton includes limbs and girdles.
Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons.
Ligaments connect bone to bone; cartilage reduces friction and absorbs shock at joints.
Skeletal muscle contraction involves actin and myosin filaments sliding past one another.
study_notes:
The axial skeleton includes the skull, vertebral column and thoracic cage; the appendicular skeleton includes limbs and
 girdles.

Ligaments connect bone to bone; cartilage reduces friction and absorbs shock at joints.
Skeletal muscle contraction involves actin and myosin filaments sliding past one another.
Antagonistic muscle pairs produce opposite movements at joints.
content.short_questions:
What is a tendon?

    Answer: A tendon is a tough connective tissue that attaches muscle to bone.

 What is an antagonistic muscle pair?

    Answer: It is a pair of muscles that produce opposite movements; when one contracts, the other generally relaxes.
content.long_questions:
Explain the sliding-filament mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction.

    Answer: A nerve impulse triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium binds to troponin, shifting
    tropomyosin and exposing binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to actin and perform power strokes using energy
    from ATP, pulling thin filaments inward. Repeated cross-bridge cycles shorten the sarcomere. Calcium reuptake allows
    relaxation.

A reflex arc provides a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus.

What is a reflex action?

    Answer: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus, commonly coordinated through a
    reflex arc.

 What is a hormone?

    Answer: A hormone is a chemical messenger released by an endocrine cell or gland that acts on target cells with

content.overview:
Human reproduction involves the formation of gametes, fertilisation, implantation, embryonic development, birth and
 parental care. The reproductive systems are regulated by hormones.
key_terms: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules; oogenesis occurs in ovarian follicles.
The menstrual cycle involves coordinated changes in the ovaries and uterine lining.
Fertilisation normally occurs in the oviduct and forms a diploid zygote.
The embryo implants in the uterine endometrium.

What is fertilisation?

    Answer: Fertilisation is the fusion of a haploid male gamete and a haploid female gamete to form a diploid zygote.

    Answer: The placenta is a temporary organ that supports exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes between maternal
    and fetal blood and also produces hormones.

    Answer: A sperm penetrates the secondary oocyte and the nuclei ultimately unite to form a diploid zygote. The zygote

content.overview:
The immune system protects the body against pathogens and abnormal cells. Innate immunity provides rapid general
 defence, while adaptive immunity develops specific responses and immunological memory.
key_terms: Physical barriers include skin and mucous membranes.
Phagocytes engulf pathogens; inflammation helps recruit immune cells.
B lymphocytes can differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells.
T lymphocytes coordinate immune responses or destroy infected cells.
study_notes: Physical barriers include skin and mucous membranes.

B lymphocytes can differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells.
T lymphocytes coordinate immune responses or destroy infected cells.

content.short_questions:
What is an antigen?

    Answer: An antigen is a substance recognised by the immune system that can trigger a specific immune response.

 What is immunological memory?

    Answer: Immunological memory is the ability of the adaptive immune system to respond more rapidly and strongly
    after a previous exposure to an antigen.
content.long_questions:
Compare innate and adaptive immunity.

    Answer: Innate immunity is present from birth, responds rapidly and recognises broad classes of threats. It includes
    barriers, phagocytes, inflammation and complement. Adaptive immunity is antigen-specific, involves B and T

 Human Body
 Chapter overview
 The immune system protects the body against pathogens and abnormal cells. Innate immunity provides rapid general
 defence, while adaptive immunity develops specific responses and immunological memory.

 Key terms
 • Physical barriers include skin and mucous membranes.

 • Phagocytes engulf pathogens; inflammation helps recruit immune cells.

 • B lymphocytes can differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells.

 Short-answer practice — model answers
 What is an antigen?

    Answer: An antigen is a substance recognised by the immune system that can trigger a specific immune response.

 What is immunological memory?

    Answer: Immunological memory is the ability of the adaptive immune system to respond more rapidly and strongly
    after a previous exposure to an antigen.

 Long-answer practice — model answer

    Answer: Innate immunity is present from birth, responds rapidly and recognises broad classes of threats. It includes
    barriers, phagocytes, inflammation and complement. Adaptive immunity is antigen-specific, involves B and T
    lymphocytes, develops after exposure and forms memory cells. This memory allows a faster, stronger response on
    subsequent exposure.
